To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) turbulence in the cloud layer is consistent with high-Reynoldsnumber flows; (2) the microphysical properties of the clouds are typical of those found in continental clouds; and (3) the cloud microphysical and turbulent properties are consistent with the observed cloud microphysics.

the observed turbulence in warm clouds is similar to that in the free atmosphere, and that the microphysical and turbulence measurements are consistent with the idea that cloud droplets are well-mixed on the scale of the turbulence.

turbulence and cloud microphysics measurements performed on mountaintops are representative of those made in free clouds, and that the turbulence–cloud interactions are consistent with expectations from theory and previous measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of turbulence and cloud microphysics in a mountainous environment.
the study of cloud–turbulent interactions and the role of turbulence in the formation of clouds.
the development of an improved understanding of the microphysical and turbulent properties of clouds, and the interactions between these two processes.
